blocks.text: The discussion will explore the themes of Ngoya’s current solo exhibition, The Sacred Fire Beneath Our Feet , and his wider practice. Ngoya has gained recognition through many institutional exhibitions in Belgium and the Netherlands, where he lives and works.

blocks.caption: Artist Anthony Ngoya and curator Christine Eyene

blocks.text: Through discarded materials and fragments of memory, Anthony Ngoya explores the fluid boundaries between personal experience, fiction and historical narratives.

Working between the Netherlands and Belgium, French artist Anthony Ngoya approaches the archive as a space of speculation and reinvention. Drawing on photography, archival footage, textiles, painting, printmaking and installation, he investigates how histories are constructed, transmitted and obscured.

Used fabrics, discarded industrial materials and fragments recovered from construction sites become the foundations of his compositions. Already imbued with histories of use, these materials take on new associations through juxtaposition, transformation, and placement. Ngoya reveals unexpected beauty in the overlooked, letting fragmented memories oscillate between the real and the imagined.
His practice invites a reconsideration of what constitutes an archive, how memory is embodied in everyday objects and how alternative forms of storytelling might expand our understanding of the past.

Christine Eyene is an art historian, curator and writer appointed curator of the 2027 cultural season at the Institut français du Cameroun. Previously a Research Curator at Tate Liverpool and Co-Director of the Exhibition Research Lab at Liverpool John Moores University, she also worked alongside Lubaina Himid on Making Histories Visible , an interdisciplinary research project exploring artistic practices and histories from African and diasporic perspectives.
The exhibition is on at the Yamamoto Keiko Rochaix, London
